questions.question: How is fmt.Errorf different from errors.New?
questions.title: errors.New versus fmt.Errorf
questions.direct_answer: `errors.New` creates an error from fixed text, while `fmt.Errorf` builds a message with formatting verbs and can wrap one or more underlying errors with `%w`. Use `errors.New` for a simple constant message and `fmt.Errorf` when the failure needs runtime context or a preserved cause.

interviewer_intent.testing: Choosing the smallest error constructor while preserving required context and identity.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating formatted text as structured error information or using `%v` when matching must survive.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate message context, wrapped identity, and typed fields as three different needs.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `fmt.Errorf` formats values such as names, IDs, and operations.
`fmt.Errorf` with `%w` preserves an underlying error for inspection.
Formatting with `%v` includes text but does not wrap the cause.
Use a custom type when callers need structured fields rather than prose.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`errors.New` and `fmt.Errorf` both produce values that satisfy `error`, but they solve different construction needs. `errors.New` stores one supplied message. `fmt.Errorf` applies formatting rules, so it can insert runtime details such as an operation, filename, or user ID without manual string building.

For example, `errors.New("user not found")` is suitable for a fixed local failure. If the message must identify user 42, `fmt.Errorf("user %d not found", id)` is clearer. If there is also an underlying database error that callers are allowed to inspect, `fmt.Errorf("load user %d: %w", id, err)` adds context and preserves that cause.

`%w` is more than display formatting. It creates an unwrap relationship that `errors.Is` and `errors.As` can traverse. `%v` prints an error's message without promising that relationship. Choosing `%w` therefore affects the API, not just the sentence shown in a log.

Neither constructor replaces a custom type when fields are part of the contract. I use fixed text for a self-contained failure, formatted text for human context, wrapping for a deliberate inspectable cause, and a type for machine-readable data. That keeps the error representation no richer—and no poorer—than callers need.

sections.title: Build errors in layers
sections.content:
Error construction has three independent dimensions: readable wording, causal identity, and structured data. A formatting function improves wording; `%w` records a cause; a custom type assigns names and types to data. One operation may need one, two, or all three.

Adding context at package boundaries makes a final message traceable, but repeating the same operation at every layer creates noise. Each wrapper should contribute information that was not already available lower down.

sections.title: Choose by information need
sections.content:
| Need | Tool | Inspectable later? |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed message | `errors.New` | Only as that value or text |
| Dynamic message | `fmt.Errorf` with ordinary verbs | Text only |
| Context plus cause | `fmt.Errorf` with `%w` | Yes, with `errors.Is` or `errors.As` |
| Named fields | Custom error type | Yes, with `errors.As` |

questions.question: What is the difference between %w and %v in fmt.Errorf?
questions.title: Wrapping with %w versus formatting with %v
questions.direct_answer: In `fmt.Errorf`, `%w` formats an error and records it as an underlying cause, so `errors.Is` and `errors.As` can find it. `%v` only copies the error's text into the new message. Use `%w` when exposing the cause is an intentional contract; use `%v` or translation when it should remain hidden.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that wrapping is semantic API behavior, not cosmetic formatting.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `%v` and expecting errors.Is to work, or wrapping dependency details unintentionally.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain both preservation and abstraction costs of `%w`.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Both `%w` and `%v` include the error text in the outer message.
Wrapping exposes the underlying error as part of observable behavior.
Translate or use `%v` when callers should not depend on an implementation detail.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Within `fmt.Errorf`, `%w` and `%v` can produce similar-looking messages, but only `%w` records an underlying error. That relationship lets `errors.Is` find a sentinel and `errors.As` find a concrete type through the outer context. `%v` converts the inner error to display text and stops there.

For example, wrapping `fs.ErrNotExist` as `fmt.Errorf("read config: %w", err)` lets a caller recognize a missing file while still seeing which operation failed. Writing the same expression with `%v` may print identical words, but `errors.Is(outer, fs.ErrNotExist)` is false because there is no cause to traverse.

Wrapping is also a compatibility choice. If a package wraps a database driver's sentinel, callers may start depending on that driver-specific identity. Replacing the database can then change observable behavior. A stable package may instead translate the failure to its own sentinel or use `%v` when only the message should cross the boundary.

I use `%w` when the underlying category or type is deliberately useful to callers and documented. I use ordinary formatting when the cause is an internal detail, and I never expect text formatting to support program decisions. The question is not which verb is newer; it is which error relationship the API promises.

sections.title: A wrapping edge is part of the error tree
sections.content:
An error produced with `%w` becomes a parent node whose child is the supplied cause. Inspection starts at the outer error and walks inward. Context remains visible at the top, while identity and fields remain reachable below.

Using `%v` creates a fresh leaf containing copied words. It has no link to the original value. This is useful when preserving abstraction matters more than exposing recovery information.

sections.title: Same text, different structure
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[inner ErrNotExist] --> B[percent w]
  B --> C[outer error with unwrap link]
  C --> D[errors.Is succeeds]
  A --> E[percent v]
  E --> F[new text-only error]
  F --> G[errors.Is fails]
```

sections.title: Compare the two verbs
sections.content:
```go
package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io/fs"
)

func main() {
    wrapped := fmt.Errorf("read config: %w", fs.ErrNotExist)
    textOnly := fmt.Errorf("read config: %v", fs.ErrNotExist)

    fmt.Println(wrapped)
    fmt.Println(errors.Is(wrapped, fs.ErrNotExist))
    fmt.Println(errors.Is(textOnly, fs.ErrNotExist))
}
```
Both errors read naturally, but the checks print `true` and `false` because only the first has an unwrap link.

questions.question: How does errors.Is find a wrapped error?
questions.title: Matching through an error chain
questions.direct_answer: `errors.Is(err, target)` examines the outer error and then traverses errors exposed through `Unwrap`, including wrapped error trees. It matches by identity or a type's shallow `Is` method, not by comparing message strings, so added context does not destroy a stable category.

interviewer_intent.testing: Traversal of error wrapping and the distinction between category and type inspection.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using direct equality on a wrapped sentinel or assuming Is compares strings.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace a multi-layer chain from service context to the original category.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `errors.Is` checks the outer error and its unwrap tree.
A `%w` wrapper exposes its underlying error to that search.
Sentinel matching is based on identity, not equal text.
Custom error types may define a shallow `Is(error) bool` method.
Use `errors.As` instead when the concrete type and fields are needed.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`errors.Is` answers whether an error represents a target category even when context has been wrapped around it. It starts with the supplied error, then follows errors returned by `Unwrap` methods through the error tree. A wrapper made by `fmt.Errorf` with `%w` participates in that traversal.

For example, a storage function can wrap `ErrNotFound` with a record key, and a service can wrap that result with `load profile`. Direct comparison with the sentinel fails at the outer layer, but `errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound)` walks through both wrappers and succeeds.

The operation does not search message text. Two errors that both print `not found` remain unrelated unless one is the target, wraps the target, or implements an appropriate `Is` method. That prevents small wording changes from breaking control flow. A custom `Is` implementation should compare only the current values and must not recursively call `Unwrap` itself.

I use `Is` when the caller needs a yes-or-no category such as not found, permission denied, or canceled. I use `errors.As` when it needs a concrete error's fields. Both require the package to preserve and document the relevant error relationship; wrapping every internal error automatically can expose more contract than intended.

sections.title: Search from context toward cause
sections.content:
Wrapping lets each layer annotate the same failure rather than replacing it. The final error can explain the complete operation while retaining a recognizable root category. Inspection walks that structure in a defined outer-to-inner order.

A single error may also unwrap to several children, forming a tree. The caller should ask a semantic question with `Is`, not manually peel one layer or assume a fixed depth.

sections.title: Traversal of a wrapped category
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[load profile wrapper] -->|Unwrap| B[record 42 wrapper]
  B -->|Unwrap| C[ErrNotFound]
  D[errors.Is target ErrNotFound] --> A
  A --> E{match?}
  E -- outer no --> B
  B --> F{match?}
  F -- wrapper no --> C
  C --> G[identity match true]
```
